VIDEO.title: Jesus' Most SAVAGE Moment (Matthew 23 Explained)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 23 · Episode 45 (#48 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: Strain out a gnat, swallow a camel
SUMMARY: The teacher reads all of Matthew 23. Speaking to the crowds and His disciples, Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses: do what they tell you, but not what they do, for they do all their deeds to be noticed by men. He forbids titles that grant honor (Rabbi, father, instructor), then pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees, laments over Jerusalem, and says, 'your house is being left to you desolate.'

Moses' seat stands for teaching authority, like a pulpit today. Jesus has no problem with what they teach but with how they live. The heavy burdens are a yoke they will not carry themselves, and 'to be noticed by men' repeats the warnings of the Sermon on the Mount (6:1, 5).

Each woe turns on irony: careful tithes of mint, dill and cumin while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness; straining out a gnat (the smallest unclean swarming thing, Leviticus 11:41) while swallowing a camel (Leviticus 11:4); clean cups, unclean hearts; whitewashed tombs. Those who honor dead prophets are the sons of those who killed them.

The woes echo the six woes of Isaiah 5:8-23 ('Woe to those who call evil good and good evil'), and the video follows an outline of them as a chiasm whose center is 23:23-24, the weightier provisions of the Law (Micah 6:8).

The lesson: when people commit themselves to hypocritical righteousness, God's word becomes distorted and His will becomes corrupted, and over time they become blind to spiritual truth. Humility is the cure.
QUOTES: When people commit themselves to hypocritical righteousness, as Jesus defines it, God's word becomes distorted and his will becomes corrupted.
Why does Jesus save his harshest critiques? Not for unbelievers, not for Rome, not for pagans, but for the religious.
That's what it means to strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.
Somewhere along the way, obedience became a performance of righteousness.

method.p: Read the seven woes as a chiasm: the parts mirror each other, and the center (23:23-24) carries the main point.

LSB_QUOTES.text: You blind guides, who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel!
But the greatest among you shall be your servant.
He has told you, O man, what is good; / And what does Yahweh require of you / But to do justice, to love lovingkindness, / And to walk humbly with your God?

src.text: saying: “The scribes and the Pharisees have seated themselves in the chair of Moses; therefore all that they tell you, do and keep, but do not do according to their deeds; for they say things and do not do them.

lines.text: The Jewish leaders have probably left after the questions of chapter 22, so Jesus speaks to the crowds and disciples. Moses' seat stands for teaching authority, the equivalent of the pulpit today.
Jesus' problem is not how they teach but how they live. The heavy burdens are a yoke, a rabbi's way of life, that they will not carry themselves (23:4).
Stone 'seats of Moses' have been found in ancient synagogues, for example at Chorazin.

left.text: But they do all their deeds to be noticed by men; for they broaden their phylacteries and lengthen the tassels of their garments.

right.text: “And when you pray, you are not to be like the hypocrites; for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that they may be seen by men.

lines.text: The same antagonist as in the Sermon on the Mount: 'unless your righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees' (5:20).
Phylacteries held Scripture from Exodus 13:9 and 16 and Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18; tassels honored Numbers 15:38-39. They made them large, to be seen.
Hypokritēs was the Greek word for a stage actor, one who plays a part.

src.text: But the greatest among you shall be your servant. And whoever exalts himself shall be humbled; and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

lines.text: The titles are not banned in themselves; Jesus corrects titles used to bestow privilege and honor. Verse 12 ends by setting humility against exaltation.
Compare 20:26-27, where the great one among you is your servant.

src.text: “But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut off the kingdom of heaven from people; for you do not enter in yourselves, nor do you allow those who are entering to go in.

lines.text: Spreading the kingdom was the very job they were meant to do, and they refuse. Instead they travel to make one proselyte, a God-fearing Gentile, and put their heavy yoke on him (23:15).
Verse 14 appears in brackets in the LSB because the earliest manuscripts lack it; it matches Mark 12:40.

src.text: “Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the sanctuary, that is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the sanctuary is obligated.’ You fools and blind men! For which is more important, the gold or the sanctuary that sanctified the gold?

lines.text: They ranked oaths upside down: the lesser thing bound you, the greater did not. If you say you will do something, just do it, as Jesus taught in Matthew 5:33-37.
The video cites a commentator: oaths by the temple or altar were thought meaningless because no lien could be put on them.

left.text: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier provisions of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness; but these are the things you should have done without neglecting the others.

right.text: ‘Now every swarming thing that swarms on the earth is detestable; it shall not be eaten.

lines.text: Mint, dill and cumin are tiny herbs; tithing them takes great precision. The gnat is the smallest unclean swarming thing, the camel the biggest unclean animal that chews the cud (Leviticus 11:4).
Justice, mercy and faithfulness run all through the Tanakh: 'to do justice, to love lovingkindness, / And to walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8).
Tithing goes back to Abram, who 'gave him a tenth of all' (Genesis 14:20).

left.text: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs which on the outside appear beautiful, but inside they are full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness.

right.text: Also, anyone who in the open field touches one who has been slain with a sword or who has died naturally, or a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean for seven days.

lines.text: Pilgrims on the way to a festival could brush against a tomb and become unclean, so tombs were whitewashed about a month before Passover. They looked clean, but the white was a warning: dead and unclean inside.
The Mishnah: on the fifteenth of Adar 'they also mark the Jewish gravesites anew' (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1), and 'graves with lime which is dissolved and poured on' (Mishnah Maaser Sheni 5:1).

left.text: so that upon you may fall the guilt of all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

right.text: So they conspired against him and at the command of the king they stoned him to death in the court of the house of Yahweh.

lines.text: They honor the dead prophets while doing what will lead to Jesus' death and His followers'. Abel to Zechariah runs from the first martyr to the last in the Old Testament, which ends with 2 Chronicles in the Hebrew order.
'I am sending you prophets' echoes God in Jeremiah 7:25: 'I have sent you all My slaves the prophets.' Jesus does what Yahweh does.

LAMENT.title: As a hen gathers her chicks

src.text: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it. Behold, your house is being left to you desolate!

lines.text: 'Jerusalem' is a metonymy, a name standing for something closely related, like 'the White House' for the president's staff. Jesus means the corrupt leaders.
He prophesies judgment on the leaders, the city and the temple.

left.text: For I say to you, from now on you will not see Me until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

right.text: The stone which the builders rejected / Has become the chief corner stone.

lines.text: Psalm 118:26 comes a few verses after 118:22, the rejected stone Jesus used in chapter 21. Israel will not see Him again until they recognize Him as the one who comes in the name of the Lord.

LAMENT.title: Woe to those who call evil good

src.text: Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, / Who substitute darkness for light and light for darkness, / Who substitute bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!

lines.text: The seven woes recall Isaiah's six (Isaiah 5:8-23), which follow the song of the vineyard, the same picture behind the parable in Matthew 21.
Feigning righteousness for self-glory sets humility aside, and without humility no one can do justice, love mercy and walk humbly with God.

TERMS.def: The seat of teaching authority; the video compares it to a pulpit.
Small boxes holding Scripture, worn on the arm and head (Exodus 13:9, 16; Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18).
Fringes on the corners of garments with a cord of blue (Numbers 15:38).
A Gentile convert to Judaism; the video says God-fearing Gentiles.
A cry of grief and judgment, as in Isaiah 5.
A tenth given to God (Genesis 14:20; Leviticus 27; Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 12; 14).
Using a name for something closely related: 'Jerusalem' for its leaders.
A mirrored pattern (A B C D C' B' A') whose center carries the main point.

WORDS.gloss: Woe! An interjection of grief or warning.
Actor, pretender, hypocrite. Look up: BDAG, ὑποκριτής.
Gehenna, hell; named for the Valley of Hinnom.
Lovingkindness, steadfast love. Look up: HALOT, חֶסֶד.

BACKGROUND.p: Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). The Mishnah says that on the fifteenth of Adar, about a month before Passover, graves were marked anew, and that graves were marked with lime poured on them (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1; Maaser Sheni 5:1).
Carved stone chairs found in ancient synagogues, such as the basalt seat from Chorazin, are often identified as the 'chair of Moses' where a teacher sat.
Small leather cases holding the four passages Exodus 13:1-10, 13:11-16, Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21. Examples have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

DEBATES.h: 'Do and keep all that they tell you'?
DEBATES.p: Some read 23:3 as real respect for the scribes' teaching from Moses; others as irony, since Jesus elsewhere warns against the teaching of the Pharisees (16:12).
Many identify him with Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20-22); others with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1), or think the two were joined in tradition.
The video follows an outline of the woes as a chiasm centered on 23:23-24. Others read them as a rising series that climaxes in the last woe and the lament.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The gnat and the camel are in Matthew 23:24 (the video says 23:4).
The rejected stone is Psalm 118:22 (the video says 18:22).
The phylacteries held four passages (Exodus 13:1-10, 13:11-16, Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21), not four verses.
Matthew says Zechariah was 'the son of Berechiah,' but the Zechariah stoned in 2 Chronicles 24 is the son of Jehoiada; the prophet Zechariah is the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1).
The video's outline of the chiasm labels six of the seven parts; the sixth woe (23:27-28) is not labeled.
The video's translation leaves out 23:14; the LSB prints it in brackets.

QUESTIONS: Why does Jesus save His harshest words for religious leaders?
What is the difference between respecting a teacher's words and copying his life?
What are the 'gnats' and the 'camels' in your own church life?
How do justice, mercy and faithfulness show up in an ordinary week?
Why does performance push out humility?
Why do you obey God: for Him, or to be seen by others?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: when people commit themselves to hypocritical righteousness, God's word becomes distorted and His will becomes corrupted, and they become blind to spiritual truth. The teachers of God's word missed God in human flesh standing in front of them because obedience became a performance. Ask why you obey God: is it for Him, or for everyone else to see? Obey in secret, and humility will let you do God's will rightly and see His activity around you.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week do one act of kindness no one will know about, and pray Micah 6:8 each morning.

- Moses' seat stands for teaching authority, like a pulpit today. Jesus has no problem with what they teach but with how they live. The heavy burdens are a yoke they will not carry themselves, and 'to be noticed by men' repeats the warnings of the Sermon on the Mount (6:1, 5).
- Each woe turns on irony: careful tithes of mint, dill and cumin while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness; straining out a gnat (the smallest unclean swarming thing, Leviticus 11:41) while swallowing a camel (Leviticus 11:4); clean cups, unclean hearts; whitewashed tombs. Those who honor dead prophets are the sons of those who killed them.
- The woes echo the six woes of Isaiah 5:8-23 ('Woe to those who call evil good and good evil'), and the video follows an outline of them as a chiasm whose center is 23:23-24, the weightier provisions of the Law (Micah 6:8).

   (video) The video cites a commentator: oaths by the temple or altar were thought meaningless because no lien could be put on them.
3. Matthew 23:23-24; Leviticus 11: A gnat and a camel
   Jesus (Matthew 23:23, LSB): "“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier provisions of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness; but these are the things you should have done without neglecting the others."
   Moses (Leviticus 11:41, LSB): "‘Now every swarming thing that swarms on the earth is detestable; it shall not be eaten."
   (video) Mint, dill and cumin are tiny herbs; tithing them takes great precision. The gnat is the smallest unclean swarming thing, the camel the biggest unclean animal that chews the cud (Leviticus 11:4). (Leviticus 11:4)
   (video) Justice, mercy and faithfulness run all through the Tanakh: 'to do justice, to love lovingkindness, / And to walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8). (Micah 6:8)
   [Background] Tithing goes back to Abram, who 'gave him a tenth of all' (Genesis 14:20). (Genesis 14:20)
4. Matthew 23:25-28; Numbers 19:16: Clean cups, whitewashed tombs
   Jesus (Matthew 23:27, LSB): "“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs which on the outside appear beautiful, but inside they are full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness."
   Moses (Numbers 19:16, LSB): "Also, anyone who in the open field touches one who has been slain with a sword or who has died naturally, or a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean for seven days."
   (video) Pilgrims on the way to a festival could brush against a tomb and become unclean, so tombs were whitewashed about a month before Passover. They looked clean, but the white was a warning: dead and unclean inside.
   [Background] The Mishnah: on the fifteenth of Adar 'they also mark the Jewish gravesites anew' (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1), and 'graves with lime which is dissolved and poured on' (Mishnah Maaser Sheni 5:1).
5. Matthew 23:29-36: From Abel to Zechariah
   Jesus (Matthew 23:35, LSB): "so that upon you may fall the guilt of all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar."
   The Chronicler (2 Chronicles 24:21, LSB): "So they conspired against him and at the command of the king they stoned him to death in the court of the house of Yahweh."
   (video) They honor the dead prophets while doing what will lead to Jesus' death and His followers'. Abel to Zechariah runs from the first martyr to the last in the Old Testament, which ends with 2 Chronicles in the Hebrew order.
   (video) 'I am sending you prophets' echoes God in Jeremiah 7:25: 'I have sent you all My slaves the prophets.' Jesus does what Yahweh does. (Jeremiah 7:25-26)

## Jerusalem, Jerusalem
1. Matthew 23:37-38: As a hen gathers her chicks
   Lament Matthew 23:37-38: "“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it. Behold, your house is being left to you desolate!" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+23:37-38
   (video) 'Jerusalem' is a metonymy, a name standing for something closely related, like 'the White House' for the president's staff. Jesus means the corrupt leaders.
   (video) He prophesies judgment on the leaders, the city and the temple.
2. Matthew 23:39; Psalm 118:22, 26: Until you say, 'Blessed'
   Jesus (Matthew 23:39, LSB): "For I say to you, from now on you will not see Me until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’”"
   The psalmist (Psalm 118:22, LSB): "The stone which the builders rejected / Has become the chief corner stone."
   (video) Psalm 118:26 comes a few verses after 118:22, the rejected stone Jesus used in chapter 21. Israel will not see Him again until they recognize Him as the one who comes in the name of the Lord. (Psalm 118:26)
3. Isaiah 5:20; Matthew 23:23: Woe to those who call evil good
   Isaiah 5 Isaiah 5:20: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, / Who substitute darkness for light and light for darkness, / Who substitute bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+5:20
   (video) The seven woes recall Isaiah's six (Isaiah 5:8-23), which follow the song of the vineyard, the same picture behind the parable in Matthew 21.
   (video) Feigning righteousness for self-glory sets humility aside, and without humility no one can do justice, love mercy and walk humbly with God.

## Key people
- The scribes and Pharisees: Sit in Moses' seat; teach rightly but live for applause. [Background] Not every religious leader was corrupt; Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea are examples.
- The crowds and the disciples: Jesus' audience once the leaders have left. [Background] The warning is for everyone who has ears to hear.
- Abel: The first righteous martyr. [Background] 'The voice of your brother's blood is crying out to Me' (Genesis 4:10).
- Zechariah: The last martyr in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 24. [Background] The Chronicler names him son of Jehoiada the priest; Matthew has 'son of Berechiah.'
- Abram and Melchizedek: The first tithe, a tenth of everything. [Background] Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High.

## Places [Background]
- Temple (named in the video): Jesus speaks in the temple courts; 'your house is being left to you desolate' (23:38).
- Kidron tombs: Monumental tombs in the Kidron Valley, later named for prophets and kings: the kind of 'monuments of the righteous' in 23:29.
- Mount of Olives: Pilgrims came over it to the city; Jesus sits there next (24:3).

## Key terms
- Chair of Moses: The seat of teaching authority; the video compares it to a pulpit.
- Phylacteries: Small boxes holding Scripture, worn on the arm and head (Exodus 13:9, 16; Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18).
- Tassels: Fringes on the corners of garments with a cord of blue (Numbers 15:38).
- Proselyte: A Gentile convert to Judaism; the video says God-fearing Gentiles.
- Woe: A cry of grief and judgment, as in Isaiah 5.
- Tithe: A tenth given to God (Genesis 14:20; Leviticus 27; Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 12; 14).
- Metonymy: Using a name for something closely related: 'Jerusalem' for its leaders.
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern (A B C D C' B' A') whose center carries the main point.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Marking graves: Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). The Mishnah says that on the fifteenth of Adar, about a month before Passover, graves were marked anew, and that graves were marked with lime poured on them (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1; Maaser Sheni 5:1).
- Seats of Moses: Carved stone chairs found in ancient synagogues, such as the basalt seat from Chorazin, are often identified as the 'chair of Moses' where a teacher sat.
- Phylacteries: Small leather cases holding the four passages Exodus 13:1-10, 13:11-16, Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21. Examples have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- 'Do and keep all that they tell you'? Some read 23:3 as real respect for the scribes' teaching from Moses; others as irony, since Jesus elsewhere warns against the teaching of the Pharisees (16:12).
- Which Zechariah? Many identify him with Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20-22); others with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1), or think the two were joined in tradition.
- A chiasm? The video follows an outline of the woes as a chiasm centered on 23:23-24. Others read them as a rising series that climaxes in the last woe and the lament.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The gnat and the camel are in Matthew 23:24 (the video says 23:4).
- The rejected stone is Psalm 118:22 (the video says 18:22).
- The phylacteries held four passages (Exodus 13:1-10, 13:11-16, Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21), not four verses.
- Matthew says Zechariah was 'the son of Berechiah,' but the Zechariah stoned in 2 Chronicles 24 is the son of Jehoiada; the prophet Zechariah is the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1).
- The video's outline of the chiasm labels six of the seven parts; the sixth woe (23:27-28) is not labeled.
- The video's translation leaves out 23:14; the LSB prints it in brackets.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does Jesus save His harshest words for religious leaders?
2. What is the difference between respecting a teacher's words and copying his life?
3. What are the 'gnats' and the 'camels' in your own church life?
4. How do justice, mercy and faithfulness show up in an ordinary week?
5. Why does performance push out humility?
6. Why do you obey God: for Him, or to be seen by others?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: when people commit themselves to hypocritical righteousness, God's word becomes distorted and His will becomes corrupted, and they become blind to spiritual truth. The teachers of God's word missed God in human flesh standing in front of them because obedience became a performance. Ask why you obey God: is it for Him, or for everyone else to see? Obey in secret, and humility will let you do God's will rightly and see His activity around you.
- Study note (added): this week do one act of kindness no one will know about, and pray Micah 6:8 each morning.
